Climate change and temperature anomalies¶

If we wanted to study climate change, we can find data on the Combined Land-Surface Air and Sea-Surface Water Temperature Anomalies in the Northern Hemisphere at NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies. The tabular data of temperature anomalies can be found here

To define temperature anomalies you need to have a reference, or base, period which NASA clearly states that it is the period between 1951-1980.

In [105]:
# Load weather data
weather = pd.read_csv("https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/tabledata_v4/NH.Ts+dSST.csv",
                      skiprows=1,
                      na_values="***")

You have two objectives in this section:

  1. Select the year and the twelve month variables from the weather dataset. We do not need the others (J-D, D-N, DJF, etc.) for this assignment.
  2. Convert the dataframe from wide to 'long' format. Name the new dataframe as tidyweather, name the variable containing the name of the month as month, and the temperature deviation values as delta.
In [106]:
# List the 12 month column names in calendar order.
month_cols = ['Jan','Feb','Mar','Apr','May','Jun',
              'Jul','Aug','Sep','Oct','Nov','Dec']

# Build a tidy ("long") version of the NASA temperature data.
# Each row will be one year-month observation.
tidyweather = (
    weather
    # Keep only the year and the monthly anomaly columns.
    .loc[:, ['Year'] + month_cols]
    # Convert from wide to long: one row per year-month.
    .melt(id_vars='Year', var_name='month', value_name='delta')
)

# Preview the result.
print(tidyweather.head())

1  1881   Jan  -0.31

3  1883   Jan  -0.58

Plotting Information¶

Let us plot the data using a time-series scatter plot, and add a trendline. To do that, we first need to create a new variable called date in order to ensure that the delta values are plot chronologically.

In [107]:
# Prepare the data: drop missing values and create a numeric date for the trend line.
plot_data = (
    tidyweather
    # Remove missing temperature readings so the regression line works cleanly.
    .dropna(subset=['delta'])
    .assign(
        # Build a real datetime from Year and month (e.g., "1880-Jan-01").
        date=lambda d: pd.to_datetime(d['Year'].astype(str) + '-' + d['month'] + '-01'),
        # matplotlib needs a numeric x-axis to fit the regression line.
        date_num=lambda d: mdates.date2num(d['date'])
    )
)

# Create the plot: scatter of anomalies over time with a fitted trend line.
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
sns.regplot(data=plot_data, x='date_num', y='delta',
            scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.3, 's': 10},
            line_kws={'color': 'red'})

# Format the numeric x-axis back into readable years.
plt.gca().xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter('%Y'))
plt.gca().xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator(20))

plt.title('Northern Hemisphere temperature anomaly over time')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Temperature anomaly (°C)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Is the effect of increasing temperature more pronounced in some months? Use faceting to produce a separate scatter plot for each month, again with a smoothing line.

In [108]:
# Put the months in calendar order so the facets are laid out sensibly.
month_order = ['Jan','Feb','Mar','Apr','May','Jun',
               'Jul','Aug','Sep','Oct','Nov','Dec']

# Prepare data and enforce month ordering.
plot_data = (
    tidyweather
    .dropna(subset=['delta'])
    .assign(month=lambda d: pd.Categorical(d['month'], categories=month_order, ordered=True))
)

# One subplot per month, each with its own regression line.
g = sns.FacetGrid(plot_data, col='month', col_wrap=3,
                  height=3, aspect=1.2, sharex=False, sharey=True)
g.map_dataframe(sns.regplot, x='Year', y='delta',
                scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.3, 's': 8},
                line_kws={'color': 'red'})
g.set_axis_labels('Year', 'Anomaly (°C)')
g.fig.suptitle('Monthly temperature anomalies with trend lines', y=1.02)
plt.show()

It is sometimes useful to group data into different time periods to study historical data. For example, we often refer to decades such as 1970s, 1980s, 1990s etc. to refer to a period of time. NASA calculates a temperature anomaly, as difference from the base period of 1951-1980.

In [109]:
# Define the year bins and human-readable labels.
interval_bins = [1880, 1920, 1950, 1980, 2010, 2030]
interval_labels = ['1881-1920', '1921-1950', '1951-1980', '1981-2010', '2011-present']

# Add an interval column using pd.cut, which assigns each year to a bucket.
comparison = (
    tidyweather
    .dropna(subset=['delta'])
    .query('Year >= 1881')
    .assign(
        interval=lambda d: pd.cut(
            d['Year'], bins=interval_bins, labels=interval_labels, right=True
        )
    )
)

So far, we have been working with monthly anomalies. However, we might be interested in average annual anomalies. We can do this by using group_by() and mean(), followed by a scatter plot to display the result.

In [111]:
# Compute the average anomaly for each year.
annual = (
    tidyweather
    .dropna(subset=['delta'])
    .groupby('Year', as_index=False)
    .agg(mean_delta=('delta', 'mean'))
)

# Plot year against the annual mean, with a trend line.
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
sns.regplot(data=annual, x='Year', y='mean_delta',
            scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.6}, line_kws={'color': 'red'})
plt.title('Average annual temperature anomaly in the Northern Hemisphere')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Mean anomaly (°C)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Confidence Interval for delta¶

NASA points out on their website that

A one-degree global change is significant because it takes a vast amount of heat to warm all the oceans, atmosphere, and land by that much. In the past, a one- to two-degree drop was all it took to plunge the Earth into the Little Ice Age.

Your task is to construct a confidence interval for the average annual delta since 2011, both using a formula and using a bootstrap simulation.

In [112]:
# Use the annual means from 2011 onward.
recent_annual = annual.query('Year >= 2011')['mean_delta']

# Sample statistics needed for the t-based confidence interval.
n = len(recent_annual)                       # number of annual observations
mean_delta = recent_annual.mean()            # sample mean
sd_delta = recent_annual.std(ddof=1)         # sample standard deviation
se_delta = sd_delta / np.sqrt(n)             # standard error of the mean
t_crit = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=n-1)          # critical value for 95% CI

# Lower and upper bounds.
ci_lower = mean_delta - t_crit * se_delta
ci_upper = mean_delta + t_crit * se_delta

print(f'Mean annual delta (2011-present): {mean_delta:.3f}°C')
print(f'95% CI via formula: [{ci_lower:.3f}, {ci_upper:.3f}]°C')

Mean annual delta (2011-present): 1.180°C
95% CI via formula: [1.035, 1.326]°C
In [113]:
# Number of bootstrap resamples.
n_boot = 10_000

# Resample the recent annual means with replacement many times,
# then take the mean of each resampled sample.
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
boot_means = (
    rng
    .choice(recent_annual, size=(n_boot, len(recent_annual)), replace=True)
    .mean(axis=1)
)

# The 95% bootstrap CI is the 2.5th and 97.5th percentile of the bootstrapped means.
boot_lower, boot_upper = np.percentile(boot_means, [2.5, 97.5])

print(f'95% CI via bootstrap: [{boot_lower:.3f}, {boot_upper:.3f}]°C')

95% CI via bootstrap: [1.049, 1.310]°C

Create a plot¶

What I would like you to do is to calculate the average net approval rate (approve- disapprove) for each week since he got into office. I want you plot the net approval for each week in 2026 along with its 95% confidence interval.

In [115]:
# Choose the presidential term year you want to visualise.
# The approval dataset currently covers 2025-2026, so 2026 is used here.
plot_year = 2026

# Build weekly summaries of net approval (approve - disapprove).
weekly_approval = (
    approval_polllist
    # Convert text dates to datetime objects.
    .assign(modeldate=lambda d: pd.to_datetime(d['modeldate']))
    # Net approval for each daily estimate.
    .assign(net_approval=lambda d: d['approve'] - d['disapprove'])
    # Group each row into the Monday that starts its week.
    .assign(week=lambda d: d['modeldate'].dt.to_period('W').dt.to_timestamp())
    # Keep only the chosen year.
    .query('modeldate.dt.year == @plot_year')
    # Summarise each week.
    .groupby('week', as_index=False)
    .agg(
        mean_net=('net_approval', 'mean'),
        sd_net=('net_approval', 'std'),
        n=('net_approval', 'count')
    )
    # Standard error and 95% confidence interval for each weekly mean.
    .assign(se=lambda d: d['sd_net'] / np.sqrt(d['n']))
    .assign(
        ci_lo=lambda d: d['mean_net'] - stats.t.ppf(0.975, d['n'] - 1) * d['se'],
        ci_hi=lambda d: d['mean_net'] + stats.t.ppf(0.975, d['n'] - 1) * d['se']
    )
)

# Plot the weekly mean and shade the 95% CI.
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
sns.lineplot(data=weekly_approval, x='week', y='mean_net')
plt.fill_between(weekly_approval['week'], weekly_approval['ci_lo'],
                 weekly_approval['ci_hi'], alpha=0.3, label='95% CI')
plt.axhline(0, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=1)
plt.title(f'Weekly net approval ({plot_year}) with 95% confidence interval')
plt.xlabel('Week')
plt.ylabel('Net approval (approve - disapprove)')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Avocados!¶

The data comes from the Hass Avocado Board and provides weekly sales (total volume in pounds (lbs) and average price in $/lb) in a number of regions around the US. You can find more about the data here https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/timmate/avocado-prices-2020

In [116]:
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Global viz/theme settings (Seaborn-first)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", palette="husl", context="talk")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Data: Hass avocado sales and prices (Kaggle)
# https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/timmate/avocado-prices-2020
# Notes:
# - 'units' = pounds in the HAB data
# - PLU codes:
#   4046: small/medium Hass (~3-5 oz)
#   4225: large Hass (~8-10 oz)
#   4770: extra large Hass (~10-15 oz)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
avocado = (
    pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kostis-christodoulou/am01-code-sep2026/main/data/avocado.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
      # drop the national aggregate so every analysis stays at the region level
      .query('region != "TotalUS"')
      .assign(
          # Make some columns categorical for efficiency and clearer semantics
          type=lambda d: d["type"].astype("category"),
          region=lambda d: d["region"].astype("category")
      )
)

avocado['date'] = pd.to_datetime(avocado['date'], dayfirst=True)

# For each week, compute each type's share of total volume.
share_by_type = (
    avocado
    .groupby(['date', 'type'], as_index=False)
    .agg(total_volume=('total_volume', 'sum'))
    # weekly total across both types
    .assign(weekly_total=lambda d: d.groupby('date')['total_volume'].transform('sum'))
    # convert to percentage
    .assign(pct=lambda d: d['total_volume'] / d['weekly_total'] * 100)
)

    .sort_values('total_volume', ascending=False)

    .assign(
        pct=lambda d: d['total_volume'] / d['total_volume'].sum() * 100,
        cum_pct=lambda d: d['pct'].cumsum()
    )
)

# Approximate price elasticity: percentage change in volume vs price.
elasticity = (
    avocado
    # national weekly totals by type
    .groupby(['date', 'type'], as_index=False)
    .agg(total_volume=('total_volume', 'sum'), mean_price=('average_price', 'mean'))
    # ensure rows are in chronological order within each type
    .sort_values(['type', 'date'])
    # percentage change from one week to the next, computed separately by type
    .assign(
        price_change=lambda d: d.groupby('type')['mean_price'].pct_change(),
        volume_change=lambda d: d.groupby('type')['total_volume'].pct_change()
    )
    # drop the first observation of each type (no previous week to compare to)
    .dropna(subset=['price_change', 'volume_change'])
)

# Scatterplot with linear fit, faceted by type.

           hue='type', col='type', height=6, aspect=1,

Challenge 1: Risk-Return Tradeoff Plot by year¶

Last week we downloaded prices of stocks from yahoo finance using yfinance and calcualted the risk-return tradeoff for each stock. However, that graph was for the toal time period. What if we wanted to produce a risk-return tradeoff for each of the past five years?

The code below will download the adjusted closing price for a few stocks from Yahoo finance. Your task is to manipulate the data and to produce a graph that look like the one below. There is no need to reproduce evry single aesthetic detail of the plot-- the key is to get your data manipulation right!

The final graph should look like this:

# =============================================================================
# 3. TURN THE DATAFRAME IN LONG FORMAT
# =============================================================================

long_df = (adj_close_df
           .reset_index()
           .melt(id_vars='Date', var_name='Ticker', value_name='Adj_Close')
           .dropna()
           .sort_values(['Ticker', 'Date'])
           .reset_index(drop=True))

long_df['Year'] = long_df['Date'].dt.year

# Simple daily return: (today / yesterday) - 1
long_df['Simple_Return'] = long_df.groupby('Ticker')['Adj_Close'].pct_change()
# Log daily return: ln(today / yesterday)
long_df['Log_Return'] = (long_df.groupby('Ticker')['Adj_Close']
                         .transform(lambda p: np.log(p / p.shift(1))))

long_df.head()

# =============================================================================
# 3. ANNUAL RISK-RETURN ANALYSIS IN LONG FORMAT
# =============================================================================
TRADING_DAYS = 252


yearly = (long_df.groupby(['Year', 'Ticker'])
          .agg(mean_simple=('Simple_Return', 'mean'),
               mean_log=('Log_Return', 'mean'),
               std_log=('Log_Return', 'std'),        # risk from LOG returns
               first_px=('Adj_Close', 'first'),
               last_px=('Adj_Close', 'last'),
               Days=('Simple_Return', 'count'))
          .reset_index())

# M1: the real point-to-point return for that year (first vs last price).
yearly['M1_point_to_point'] = yearly['last_px'] / yearly['first_px'] - 1
# M2 / M3 / M4: the shortcuts, but averaged WITHIN the year only.
yearly['M2_yearly'] = yearly['mean_simple'] * TRADING_DAYS
yearly['M3_yearly'] = yearly['mean_log'] * TRADING_DAYS
yearly['M4_yearly'] = np.exp(yearly['M3_yearly']) - 1
# Annualised risk for that single year, from LOG returns.
yearly['Risk_yearly'] = yearly['std_log'] * np.sqrt(TRADING_DAYS)

yearly.head()



# Annualize metrics

annual_metrics = yearly.assign(
    Annual_Return=np.exp(yearly['mean_log'] * TRADING_DAYS) - 1,
    Annual_Risk=yearly['std_log'] * np.sqrt(TRADING_DAYS),
)

print("--- Annual Risk-Return Metrics (Tidy Format) ---")
print(annual_metrics[['Year', 'Ticker', 'Annual_Return', 'Annual_Risk']]
      .head(10).to_string())



# =============================================================================
# 4. PLOTTING WITH SEABORN AND DIRECT LABELS (MODIFIED)
# ==========================================
# sns.set_style("whitegrid")
print("Generating plot...")
g = sns.relplot(
    data=annual_metrics,
    x='Annual_Risk',
    y='Annual_Return',
    hue='Ticker',
    col='Year',
    col_wrap=3,
    s=150,
    alpha=0.8,
    height=5,
    aspect=1.2,
    kind='scatter',
    legend=False,
    facet_kws={'sharey': False}   # let each year's panel auto-scale its own y-axis
)

for year, ax in g.axes_dict.items():
    ax.set_title(f"Year: {year}")
    year_data = annual_metrics[annual_metrics['Year'] == year]

    # Direct text label next to each point
    for idx, row in year_data.iterrows():
        ax.annotate(
            text=row['Ticker'],
            xy=(row['Annual_Risk'], row['Annual_Return']),
            color='black',
            size=9,
            weight='normal',
            xytext=(7, 0),
            textcoords='offset points'
        )

    # Percent-format the axes and add reference lines
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mticker.PercentFormatter(1.0, decimals=0))
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mticker.PercentFormatter(1.0, decimals=0))
    ax.axhline(0, ls='--', color='gray', zorder=0)

    if not year_data.empty:
        median_risk = year_data['Annual_Risk'].median()
        ax.axvline(median_risk, ls=':', color='gray', zorder=0, label='Median Risk')

title_str = (f"Annual Risk vs. Return by Year\n"
             f"Data from {start_date.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')} to {end_date.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}")
g.fig.suptitle(title_str, fontsize=18)
g.fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.02, 1, 0.95])

plt.show()

Challenge 2: Yield Curve Challenge¶
We have downloaded data on the US yield curve from 1960 to last month


Yield curve inversion occurs when short-term interest rates (3 months) exceed long-term rates (10 years), creating a downward-sloping yield curve instead of the normal upward slope.


This unusual pattern has historically preceded most U.S. recessions, making it a closely watched economic indicator.


The code below will download the data on the yield curve from FRED-- eg, the 10 year bond is at https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS10. I got dates for US recessions from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_recessions_in_the_United_States and have added them in a recessions dataframe for you.


Your task is to manipulate the data and to produce a graph that look like the one below. There is no need to reproduce every single aesthetic detail of the plot-- the key is to get your data manipulation right. Besides your code, please explain how you approached this issue


The final graph should look like this:



















In [132]:






# --- Data Preparation ---

# Get a list of FRED codes for US rates and US yield curve; choose monthly frequency
tickers = [
    'TB3MS',  # 3-month Treasury bill (or T-bill)
    'TB6MS',  # 6-month
    'GS1',    # 1-year
    'GS2',    # 2-year, etc....
    'GS3',
    'GS5',
    'GS7',
    'GS10',
    'GS20',
    'GS30'    #.... all the way to the 30-year rate
]

# Turn FRED codes to human readable variables
myvars = [
    '3-Month Treasury Bill',
    '6-Month Treasury Bill',
    '1-Year Treasury Rate',
    '2-Year Treasury Rate',
    '3-Year Treasury Rate',
    '5-Year Treasury Rate',
    '7-Year Treasury Rate',
    '10-Year Treasury Rate',
    '20-Year Treasury Rate',
    '30-Year Treasury Rate'
]

maturity = ['3m', '6m', '1y', '2y', '3y', '5y', '7y', '10y', '20y', '30y']

# Create a lookup dataframe
mylookup = pd.DataFrame({
    'symbol': tickers,
    'var': myvars,
    'maturity': maturity
})

# Display the lookup table
print("--- Lookup Table ---")
print(mylookup)
print("\n")

# Use a function for a cleaner pipe
def prepare_yield_curve_data(df, lookup):
    """
    This function takes the raw data from FRED and the lookup table,
    and returns a clean, long-format DataFrame.
    """
    return (
        df
        .reset_index() # Turn the 'DATE' index into a column
        .rename(columns={'DATE': 'date'})
        # Melt the dataframe from wide to long format
        .melt(id_vars='date', var_name='symbol', value_name='value')
        # Merge with the lookup table to get human-readable names
        .merge(lookup, on='symbol')
        # Convert 'maturity' and 'var' to ordered categorical types
        # This is similar to R's factor() with specified levels
        .assign(
            maturity=lambda x: pd.Categorical(x['maturity'], categories=maturity, ordered=True),
            duration=lambda x: pd.Categorical(x['var'], categories=myvars, ordered=True)
        )
    )

# Fetch the data from FRED and process it using a chain of commands
yield_curve = (
    web.DataReader(tickers, 'fred', start='1960-01-01')
    .pipe(prepare_yield_curve_data, mylookup)
)

print("--- Yield Curve Data (First 5 Rows) ---")
print(yield_curve.head())
print("\n")

# Use a function to pivot and calculate inversion metrics
def calculate_inversion(df):
    """Pivots data to wide format and calculates yield curve spreads."""
    return (
        df
        .pivot_table(index='date', columns='symbol', values='value')
        .assign(
            spread_10y_3m = lambda x: x['GS10'] - x['TB3MS'],
            up=lambda x: np.where(x['spread_10y_3m'] >= 0, x['spread_10y_3m'], 0),
            down=lambda x: np.where(x['spread_10y_3m'] < 0, x['spread_10y_3m'], 0)
        )
        .reset_index()
    )

yield_curve_wide = yield_curve.pipe(calculate_inversion)

print("--- Wide Yield Curve Data with Inversion (First 5 Rows) ---")
print(yield_curve_wide.head())

             "2007-12-01", "2020-02-01"],

           "1975-03-01", "1980-07-01", "1982-11-01", "1991-03-01", "2001-11-01",
           "2009-06-01", "2020-04-01"]
}).pipe(lambda df: df.assign(

))
